title: Private VPC deployment performance playbook workshop
summary: Deep dive covering Private VPC deployment design patterns for low-latency inference: DNS/eDNS, PrivateLink endpoints, NAT/egress strategies, MTU and path MTU issues, TLS termination, KV cache behavior across AZs, batching and quantization tradeoffs. Agreed to run a two-week pilot with benchmark harness and share network runbook and security artifacts.
topics: PrivateLink vs public egress for model traffic
DNS and split-horizon resolver behavior (Route53 + onprem)
NAT gateway hairpinning and egress path performance
KV cache consistency and cross-AZ latency impact
Batch size recommendations and latency SLOs
Quantization/precision effects on throughput and tail latency
TLS termination and mTLS for private deployments
Benchmarking plan and observability traces to collect
next_steps: Redwood to share VPC runbook + example CloudFormation/ARM for PrivateLink and route tables by 2026-02-24
VectorMed to provision test VPC and provide peering/endpoint config by 2026-03-02
Schedule 2-hour benchmark run with 95/99 latency targets and payloads (Redwood + VectorMed) week of 2026-03-08
Exchange perf traces (tcpdump + jaeger + rt-profiles) after initial pilot run
action_items: Alex Chen - send security pack (SOC2 + pen test summary + network diagrams) - 2026-02-23
Maya Patel - share recommended batching/kv cache config + quantization matrix - 2026-02-24
Noah Carter - create test VPC and share Terraform state (sanitized) - 2026-03-02
Evan Li - enable packet captures on egress path during pilot (store on S3) - 2026-03-10
header:
Date: Thu Feb 19 2026 14:00 EST
Duration: 75 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Diego Ramos (Redwood Infra), Jules Tran (Redwood Solutions), Priya Singh (VectorMed Head of ML), Noah Carter (VectorMed Platform), Samira Hussein (VectorMed Security), Evan Li (VectorMed SRE), Ralf Becker (VectorMed Networking)
transcript:
[00:00] Alex (Redwood): alright everyone thanks for carving out the time. goal for today is a practical playbook for private VPC deploys — networking and runtime performance tradeoffs; we want to leave with a pilot plan.
[00:18] Priya (VectorMed): thanks Alex. we saw some tail latency spikes when we moved traffic into our private subnet — hoping to figure out where that's coming from.
[00:26] Maya (Redwood SE): quick clarifying q: are you using PrivateLink endpoints into our control plane or are you planning direct internet egress through NAT?
[00:33] Noah (VectorMed): initially PrivateLink for the control plane, but model traffic, we're debating. security prefers no internet egress but ops worries about throughput and costs on NAT.
[00:44] Alex: good. we'll go through options: PrivateLink for API, TLS termination at your edge vs at Redwood, and then egress patterns.
[00:52] Jules (Redwood): also want to call out KV cache behavior — if your app is chatty across AZs the KV misses add 10s of ms which becomes visible at p99.
[01:05] Ralf (VectorMed): when you say KV misses across AZs, are we talking cross-az gc or routing? we have cross-az NAT gateways.
[01:12] Diego (Redwood Infra): yeah, two things — cross-AZ network hop + TCP handshake variance. KV cache is in-memory on the host running the model. if requests hit a different host you pay the cold-kv miss for the prefix and for the KV retrieve which can be 15-40ms depending on payload and kernel path.
[01:29] Samira (VectorMed Security): for us encryption at rest and in flight is must — any recommendations for KMS/HSM integrations with Private deployments?
[01:37] Maya: we support KMS integrations (AWS KMS and external HSM for on-prem). for PrivateLink the control plane has mTLS by default; you can choose to terminate TLS on your egress gateway to inspect. keep in mind terminating and re-encrypting adds CPU and latency.
[01:52] Priya: could that explain some of our higher tail latency when we had a proxy doing TLS inspect?
[01:57] Diego: yep, TLS inspect in the path adds unpredictable CPU jitter and packet reassembly costs, plus the MTU reduction on some proxies can cause fragmentation which hurts throughput for big token batches.
[02:11] Noah: interesting, we did have a sidecar proxy that did TLS+WAF. we can try bypassing in the test VPC.
[02:18] Alex: plan that — for pilot have a bypass path that mirrors traffic so security can still inspect a copy out-of-band. that usually helps isolate runtime impact.
[02:27] [02:30] Priya: on batching — what sizes are realistic for 16k context models? we saw latency jump when going from batch 1 to batch 4.
[02:36] Maya: expected. batching helps throughput but increases tail. for 16k contexts typical guidance: keep interactive QoS at batch size 1-2 for <50ms extra latency, batch 4-8 for throughput-heavy scoring jobs. also auto-shed based on queue depth — Redwood runtime can cap batch size by latency budget.
[02:53] Priya: we use mixed workloads — interactive chat + nightly embeddings. can we use separate routes?
[02:58] Jules: yes route based on model and priority, put embeddings through dedicated capacity with higher batch tolerance. cheap wins: different model profiles and quantization per route.
[03:08] Evan (SRE): quick network question: PrivateLink endpoints are supported but does that avoid NAT egress charges?
[03:14] Alex: PrivateLink keeps traffic inside the backbone to the control plane; model inference data still needs a route. If you pin to a private deployment in your VPC, traffic stays local to your VPC and no public NAT is used. If you call hosted endpoints via PrivateLink you'll still have regional egress when crossing account boundaries in some clouds — depends on provider.
[03:32] Ralf: we run AWS with cross-account PrivateLink to Redwood — we've already blocked public internet on our instances. we saw DNS timeouts occasionally.
[03:40] Maya: DNS is a frequent culprit — split-horizon Route53 and onprem resolvers can lead to stale negative caches. ensure your resolver TTLs, and if you're using VPC resolver endpoints check the EDNS and packet size, some onprem resolvers truncate responses causing fallback to TCP which is costly.
[03:58] Noah: ah we had that exact TCP fallback — that explains 200ms spikes.
[04:03] Diego: also watch for MTU mismatches across VPN/Direct Connect — PMTU blackhole leads to retransmits and big increases in p99. enable path MTU discovery and test with large UDP/TCP probes.
[04:16] Samira: any specific firewall rules or route table patterns you recommend?
[04:20] Alex: keep stateful egress where possible, avoid asymmetric routing. for PrivateLink create dedicated route tables per endpoint and avoid overlapping CIDRs with onprem. Document explicit IP ranges for model-serving hosts so security can whitelist rather than open 0/0.
[04:37] [04:45] Priya: on the runtime side — quantization: we tested 4-bit and saw faster throughput but occasional hallucination-like outputs; how do you recommend validating?
[04:53] Maya: quantization affects logits and numeric stability. we recommend an eval suite with golden prompt sets across SLO targets. run production-like prompt sets and measure semantic similarity and calibration. Redwood Optimize gives a quantization matrix by model/workload — we can share that.
[05:08] Priya: great. also curious about how KV cache interacts with quantized kernels?
[05:12] Diego: generally KV cache is independent of compute precision; however if quantization changes the model's attention distribution slightly you might see different cache hit patterns because tokenization/normalization quirks surface. it's subtle but worth testing.
[05:26] Jules: on autoscaling — if you scale horizontally across AZs you need sticky routing for KV locality or a shared fast kv-sync. Recommendation: prefer AZ-local hosts with warm-up pre-warming and a shared warm-KV prefetch when moving state.
[05:41] Evan: what about using a dedicated redis-like cache for KV across hosts?
[05:45] Maya: you can but then you trade network latency for consistency. remote redis will add 2–6ms typical in-region; that might be acceptable vs a 30ms cold local miss. but it's extra operational complexity and a single point to scale.
[05:59] Priya: for our use case we care a lot about 99th percentile — prefer local low-latency.
[06:04] Diego: then we should prototype sticky session routing + prefetching and small batch sizes to reduce tail.
[06:11] [06:20] Noah: logging/observability: what traces should we collect during the pilot to diagnose KV misses vs network?
[06:25] Maya: collect per-request timeline with these spans: client socket connect, TLS handshake, DNS lookup, route table hop (if available), Redwood runtime enqueue, batch formation, model forward pass, KV lookup, token emit. Include token-level latency samples for a few requests. We prefer jaeger or honeycomb style traces plus tcpdump on egress for suspected MTU/DNS failure.
[06:47] Alex: we will provide a perf-runner that injects load and captures these spans. Also we'll share a spreadsheet of proposed payloads — short chat, long chat 8–12k tokens, multi-turn and batch scoring.
[06:59] Priya: ok that helps. on security docs — Samira wants the audit trail, RBAC, and pen-test summary.
[07:06] Samira: also compliance: we need to know retention options for logs and how to redact PHI.
[07:11] Alex: Redwood supports route-level retention and token masking, we will send the security pack with details and a sample SIEM integration for audit logs.
[07:19] Ralf: network practical: we saw occasional checksum errors on our Direct Connect; what's Redwood's suggestion for verifying path integrity?
[07:25] Diego: run continuous pcap with sequence number analysis, enable TCP keepalive stats and check for RX/TX errors on NICs; also verify jumbo frames/MTU settings end-to-end. We had a customer who mismatched MTU on their firewall and it introduced 100–200ms outliers.
[07:40] [07:50] Priya: let's talk pilot scope — what minimal infra do we need? suggestions?
[07:55] Jules: minimal is 3 hosts across 2 AZs, dedicated route table for RW endpoints, PrivateLink for control plane, NAT bypass mirror for TLS-inspect, and a bench runner. We can run with either your infra or Redwood-provisioned infra in your VPC with IAM role.
[08:11] Alex: timeline: perf harness in 1 week, infra ready in 2, bench in 3 — matches next steps.
[08:18] Noah: acceptance criteria: p95 < 120ms, p99 < 350ms for chat workloads at expected QPS (we supplied a QPS target of 12 rps sustained).
[08:27] Maya: we'll capture p50/p95/p99 and token-level cost breakdown to show batching and KV share. Also we'll run a quantization AB test and show quality metrics.
[08:36] Samira: last ops question — how do you handle emergency failover if one AZ degrades?
[08:40] Diego: we do policy-based routing to fallback to nearby AZ and can auto-failover to a lower-capacity model variant (smaller quantized) to keep latency bounded; that's part of Redwood's smart-routing. we'll show config for canary/fallback policies.
[08:53] [09:00] Priya: perfect. thanks, this was very actionable.
[09:05] Alex: recap: Redwood sends runbook, batching/quant matrix, security pack; VectorMed sets up test VPC and shares sanitized TF; schedule bench run week of 2026-03-08.
[09:18] Jules: I'll also add an example nginx egress bypass and capture playbook.
[09:24] Priya: thanks everyone. we'll sync after we get the runbook.
[09:28] Alex: end of call.
